ei.title: Katherine Johnson, a "Computer" Who Looked Beyond Numbers
ei.subject: 공통영어2

fullPassage: Katherine Johnson was born on August 26, 1918, in West Virginia, in the U.S., and was the youngest of four children in a black family. Katherine was a math prodigy from early childhood. Reflecting on her youth, Katherine once said, "I counted everything — the steps to the road, the steps up to church, the number of dishes, spoons, and forks I washed." She excitedly added, "I couldn't wait to get to high school to take algebra and geometry." But Katherine's hometown had a segregated education system, and black students could not enter high school. So her father moved the family 200 kilometers away so that she could enter high school. After graduating from high school in 1932, she was admitted to a black college at the age of fifteen. By her junior year, she had taken all the math courses the college could offer. Her mentor gladly offered special classes just for her, but he was not happy when he had to tell his outstanding student about her career opportunities. "You would make a good research mathematician," he told his seventeen-year-old student, "and I'm going to prepare you for this career." Katherine asked, "Where will I find a job?" "That," he replied, "will be your problem." The path ahead was unclear and full of obstacles, but Katherine knew she had the strength to make her own way. In 1935, at the age of eighteen, Katherine graduated from college with highest honors and began her career as a teacher at a black public school. At that time, teaching was the only option available to her. It was not until 1953 that Katherine found a job at a NASA field center in Virginia. There, she worked as one of the "Black computers" who did complex calculations manually to support white male engineers. Though they greatly contributed to the space project, they endured a lot of discrimination, including segregation in the office and being referred to with terms like "girl" despite being professional women. Two weeks into the job, Katherine was reassigned to NASA's elite space research division. There, she was the only black female member of the staff. Despite her enormous contributions, the important research meetings were held only among white staff members. When she asked for permission to attend the meetings, her male colleagues said that "the girls" didn't usually go. Katherine asked, "Is there a law that says I can't go?" The embarrassed male workers had no choice but to let her in. By asking questions no one had ever asked, Katherine ended a discriminatory custom. She had faced barriers, but her efforts to overcome them paid off. She felt proud and continued her work with courage. In 1960, she wrote a research paper with another engineer about how to place a spacecraft into orbit. That was the first time a woman in her division received credit as an author of a research report. Katherine's remarkable calculations by hand were trusted more than digital computers. In early 1962, John Glenn, one of the pioneering American astronauts, was preparing to orbit the Earth for the first time in American history. NASA used an electronic computer, first introduced into the space program a year earlier, to calculate the spaceship's trajectory, but it made many minor errors. Glenn, who was concerned about its accuracy, asked Katherine Johnson to double-check the machine's figures by hand. "If she says the numbers are good," he said, "I'm good to go." Using only a pencil and a slide rule, Katherine spent a day and a half checking the calculations and finally made sure of them. Eventually, Glenn became the first American astronaut to orbit the Earth. Katherine was also part of the team that performed calculations for Apollo 11, which sent the first three men to the Moon in 1969, and even the plan to put people on Mars, which is still being worked on today. Katherine retired in 1986 after thirty-three years at NASA. After that, she dedicated the rest of her life to championing access to STEM education for Black girls. For her contributions, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015 and said, "Katherine G. Johnson refused to be limited by society's expectations of her gender and race while expanding the boundaries of humanity's reach." In 2017, NASA dedicated a building in her honor in Virginia and named it the Katherine G. Johnson Computational Research Facility. She died on February 24, 2020, at the age of 101, but her pioneering legacy will never be forgotten.

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ② beginning → began: graduated와 and로 병렬인 주절 동사 자리이므로 과거시제 began
det.analysis:
① to make: 'she had the strength to make her own way'에서 명사 strength를 꾸미는 형용사적 용법의 to부정사 to make가 맞아요. ✅ 올바름

② beginning → 여기가 정답(틀린 곳)! 'Katherine graduated from college with highest honors and ___ her career as a teacher'에서 and는 앞의 과거동사 graduated와 병렬로 동사를 이어요. 따라서 과거시제 began으로 써야 해요. beginning(분사)은 동사 자리에 올 수 없어 틀려요. ❌ beginning은 틀림 ←정답

③ available: 'teaching was the only option available to her'에서 명사 option을 뒤에서 꾸미는 형용사 available이 맞아요(후치 수식). ✅ 올바름

④ did: 'the "Black computers" who did complex calculations manually'에서 주격 관계대명사 who의 동사로, 과거 사실이라 did가 맞아요. ✅ 올바름
det.tip: graduated and began: 등위접속사 and로 이어진 과거동사 병렬

det.korean: ① Although → Despite: 뒤에 명사구(her enormous contributions)가 오므로 전치사 Despite

④ to overcome: 'her efforts to overcome them paid off'에서 명사 efforts를 꾸미는 to부정사 to overcome이 맞아요. ✅ 올바름
det.tip: 명사구 앞 전치사 Despite ↔ 절 앞 접속사 Although

det.korean: ④ which are → which is: 선행사가 단수 the plan이므로 단수 동사 is
det.analysis:
① Using: 'Using only a pencil and a slide rule, Katherine spent a day and a half checking'에서 분사구문의 현재분사 Using이 맞아요(캐서린이 사용하는 능동). ✅ 올바름

✅ ③ endured: 'they endured a lot of discrimination(많은 차별을 견뎌냈다)'이라는 문맥에 적절
✅ ④ reassigned: 'Katherine was reassigned to NASA's elite space research division(엘리트 부서로 재배치되었다)'이라는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: did complex calculations manually(손으로 계산했다) ↔ automatically(자동으로)

Katherine was also part of the team that ④<u>performed</u> calculations for Apollo 11, which sent the first three men to the Moon in 1969, and even the plan to put people on Mars, which is still being worked on today. det.korean: ① doubted → trusted: 캐서린의 손 계산은 디지털 컴퓨터보다 더 '신뢰받았다(trusted)'
det.analysis:
❌ ① doubted(의심받는) → trusted(신뢰받는): 'Katherine's remarkable calculations by hand were trusted more than digital computers'에서 그녀의 손 계산이 디지털 컴퓨터보다 더 '신뢰받았다'는 뜻이고, 바로 뒤에 글렌이 그녀에게 재확인을 요청하는 내용이 이어지므로 trusted가 맞다. doubted는 정반대라 부적절 ← 정답
✅ ② concerned: 'Glenn, who was concerned about its accuracy(정확도를 걱정한 글렌)'라는 문맥에 적절
✅ ③ Eventually: 'Eventually, Glenn became the first American astronaut(결국 최초의 미국 우주 비행사가 되었다)'라는 문맥에 적절
✅ ④ performed: 'the team that performed calculations for Apollo 11(아폴로 11호 계산을 수행한 팀)'이라는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: were trusted more than digital computers(컴퓨터보다 더 신뢰받았다) ↔ doubted(의심받는)

det.korean: 빈칸에 paid off(결실을 맺었다)가 적절
det.analysis:
❌ ① gave up(포기했다): 뒤에 '자부심을 느끼고 용기를 갖고 일을 계속했다'는 긍정 흐름과 반대

❌ ④ fell apart(무너졌다): 노력이 결실을 맺은 긍정 흐름과 반대

questions.passage: Katherine Johnson was born on August 26, 1918, in West Virginia, in the U.S., and was the youngest of four children in a black family. Katherine was a math prodigy from early childhood. Reflecting on her youth, Katherine once said, "I counted everything — the steps to the road, the steps up to church, the number of dishes, spoons, and forks I washed." She excitedly added, "I couldn't wait to get to high school to take algebra and geometry." But Katherine's hometown had a segregated education system, and black students could not enter high school. So her father moved the family 200 kilometers away so that she could enter high school. After graduating from high school in 1932, she was admitted to a black college at the age of fifteen. By her junior year, she had taken all the math courses the college could offer. Her mentor gladly offered special classes just for her, but he was not happy when he had to tell his outstanding student about her career opportunities. "You would make a good research mathematician," he told his seventeen-year-old student, "and I'm going to prepare you for this career." Katherine asked, "Where will I find a job?" "That," he replied, "will be your problem." The path ahead was unclear and full of obstacles, but Katherine knew she had the strength to make her own way.

det.korean: ③ A Mathematician Who Broke Barriers and Reached the Stars(장벽을 깨고 별에 다다른 수학자)

❌ ① The Machine That Never Made a Single Error(단 한 번도 오류를 내지 않은 기계): 본문은 전자 컴퓨터가 'many minor errors'를 냈다고 했어요.

❌ ② Why Quiz Shows Lost Their Popularity(퀴즈 쇼가 인기를 잃은 이유): 본문에 없는 내용이에요.

✅ ③ A Mathematician Who Broke Barriers and Reached the Stars(장벽을 깨고 별에 다다른 수학자): 차별(barriers)을 극복하고 우주 탐사(stars)에 기여한 캐서린을 압축한 제목이에요 ←정답

❌ ④ The End of Human Space Exploration(인간 우주 탐사의 종말): 본문 내용과 무관해요.
det.tip: 핵심 = 장벽을 깨고 우주(별) 탐사에 기여한 수학자

questions.passage: After graduating from high school in 1932, she was admitted to a black college at the age of fifteen. By her junior year, she had taken all the math courses the college could offer. Her mentor gladly offered special classes just for her, but he was not happy when he had to tell his outstanding student about her career opportunities. "You would make a good research mathematician," he told his seventeen-year-old student, "and I'm going to prepare you for this career." Katherine asked, "Where will I find a job?" "That," he replied, "<u>will be your problem</u>." The path ahead was unclear and full of obstacles, but Katherine knew she had the strength to make her own way. In 1935, at the age of eighteen, Katherine graduated from college with highest honors and began her career as a teacher at a black public school.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 will be your problem이 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: ① 일자리를 찾는 일은 그녀 스스로 해결해야 할 몫이라는 것
det.analysis:
밑줄 'will be your problem'은 캐서린이 '어디에서 일자리를 찾을 수 있을까요?(Where will I find a job?)'라고 묻자 멘토가 한 대답이에요. 당시 흑인 여성에게 일자리를 알선해 줄 수 없던 현실에서, 일자리 찾기는 그녀 스스로 감당해야 할 몫이라는 뜻이에요.

✅ ① 일자리를 찾는 것은 그녀 스스로 해결해야 할 몫이라는 뜻이에요 ←정답

❌ ② 멘토는 오히려 그녀를 '훌륭한 연구 수학자'로 평가했어요.

❌ ③ 멘토는 일자리를 직접 구해 주겠다고 하지 않고 '그게 너의 문제'라고 했어요.

❌ ④ 뒤에 'The path ahead was unclear and full of obstacles'가 이어져 어려움이 많았음을 보여줘요.
det.tip: Where will I find a job? → That will be your problem: 스스로 해결해야 할 몫

ch: 일자리를 찾는 일은 그녀 스스로 해결해야 할 몫이라는 것

questions.passage: It was not until 1953 that Katherine found a job at a NASA field center in Virginia. There, she worked as one of the "Black computers" who did complex calculations manually to support white male engineers. Though <u>they</u> greatly contributed to the space project, they endured a lot of discrimination, including segregation in the office and being referred to with terms like "girl" despite being professional women. Two weeks into the job, Katherine was reassigned to NASA's elite space research division. There, she was the only black female member of the staff.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 they가 가리키는 대상으로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: ② 복잡한 계산을 수동으로 수행한 '흑인 컴퓨터'들
det.analysis:
밑줄 문장: 'Though they greatly contributed to the space project, they endured a lot of discrimination.'(그들은 우주 프로젝트에 크게 기여했지만 많은 차별을 견뎌냈다). 앞 문장 'she worked as one of the "Black computers" who did complex calculations manually to support white male engineers'에서 소개한 '흑인 컴퓨터'들을 they가 받아요.

❌ ① 백인 남성 엔지니어들은 이들이 '지원한(support)' 대상이에요.

✅ ② 복잡한 계산을 수동으로 수행한 '흑인 컴퓨터'들: 차별을 견뎌낸 바로 그 사람들이에요 ←정답

❌ ③ 중요한 연구 회의에 참석한 백인 직원들은 뒤에 나오는 다른 집단이에요.

❌ ④ 지구 궤도를 돈 우주 비행사들은 이 문장의 대상이 아니에요.
det.tip: the "Black computers" who did ~ → they(그들)로 이어집니다.

ch: 우주 프로젝트를 이끌었던 백인 남성 엔지니어들

questions.passage: Katherine's remarkable calculations by hand were trusted more than digital computers. In early 1962, John Glenn, one of the pioneering American astronauts, was preparing to orbit the Earth for the first time in American history. NASA used an electronic computer, first introduced into the space program a year earlier, to calculate the spaceship's trajectory, but it made many minor errors. Glenn, who was concerned about __________, asked Katherine Johnson to double-check the machine's figures by hand. "If she says the numbers are good," he said, "I'm good to go." Using only a pencil and a slide rule, Katherine spent a day and a half checking the calculations and finally made sure of them.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 빈칸에 its accuracy(그것의 정확도)가 적절
det.analysis:
✅ ① its accuracy(그것의 정확도): 전자 컴퓨터가 사소한 오류를 많이 내자, 글렌이 그것의 '정확도'를 걱정해 캐서린에게 수치를 손으로 재확인해 달라고 요청했다는 문맥에 적절. 뒤에 'to double-check the machine's figures'가 이어짐 ← 정답
❌ ② its price(그것의 가격): 재확인 요청과 무관
❌ ③ its color(그것의 색): 문맥과 무관
❌ ④ its weight(그것의 무게): 문맥과 무관
det.tip: concerned about its accuracy ~ to double-check the figures: 정확도를 걱정해 재확인
